extracted.intended_audience: applicants and practitioners filing or prosecuting international design (Hague) applications; USPTO practitioners and examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive requirements for filing, fee payment, representation, correspondence, relief, conversion, and national examination of international design applications under the Hague Agreement as processed by the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribed fees for international design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application shall be subject to the payment of the following fees: (i) a basic fee; (ii) a standard designation fee in respect of each designated Contracting Party that has not made a declaration under Article 7(2) of the 1999 Act or under Rule 36(1); (iii) an individual designation fee in respect of each designated Contracting Party that has made a declaration under Article 7(2) of the 1999 Act or under Rule 36(1); (iv) a publication fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fee Calculation Sheet (DM/1) specifies amounts of basic, publication, designation, and additional word fees. The International Bureau provides an online Hague System Fee Calculator. Standard vs individual designation fees and amounts are set in the IB Schedule of Fees and on IB websites. An additional per-word fee applies where the description exceeds 100 words (based on Item 9 of DM/1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard designation fee levels and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of the standard designation fee shall be: (i) level one for Contracting Parties whose office does not carry out any examination on substantive ground; (ii) level two for Contracting Parties whose office carries out examination on substantive grounds, other than as to novelty; (iii) level three for Contracting Parties whose office carries out substantive examination including novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any Contracting Party entitled to level two or three may notify the Director General in a declaration; a Contracting Party may opt for level two even if entitled to level three. Declarations take effect three months after receipt (or later date) and may be withdrawn (one-month effect). In absence of declaration or after withdrawal, level one is deemed applicable. Standard designation fee levels are listed in the Schedule of Fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of fee payment
rubrics_metrics.description: The fees referred to (basic, standard/individual designation, publication) are, subject to exceptions, payable at the time of filing the international application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the international application contains a request for deferment of publication, the publication fee may be paid later in accordance with Rule 16(3)(a). Individual designation fees for some Contracting Parties (e.g., U.S.) may be payable in two parts (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual designation fee payable in two parts (United States example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration under Article 7(2) may specify that the individual designation fee comprises two parts: the first part to be paid at the time of filing the international application and the second part to be paid at a later date determined according to the law of the Contracting Party concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States has made such a declaration: the U.S. first part consists of the combined basic filing, search, and examination fees (established in Swiss currency under Hague Rule 28) and the second part is the issue fee payable within the period specified in a notice of allowance. Both parts are discounted for small and micro entities; payment of the small-entity first part to the IB is treated as a written assertion of small entity status. See MPEP § 2920.06 and 37 CFR 1.1031(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmittal fee when filing through the USPTO (office of indirect filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: International design applications filed through the USPTO as an office of indirect filing are subject to payment of a transmittal fee. Payment of the transmittal fee must be in U.S. dollars. The USPTO will not transmit the international design application to the International Bureau if the transmittal fee has not been paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transmittal fee is discounted for small and micro entities; payment of the exact small-entity transmittal fee is treated as a written assertion of entitlement to small entity status. See 37 CFR 1.1031(a), 1.27, 1.29 and MPEP §§ 509.*. Applicants are cautioned that an international design application not received by the IB within six months of USPTO receipt will not be entitled to a filing date as of the USPTO receipt date (Hague Rule 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of international fees through the USPTO — limitations and currency conversion risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain international fees payable to the International Bureau may be paid through the USPTO provided such fees are paid no later than the date of payment of the transmittal fee; payment through the USPTO must be in U.S. dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are not required to pay through the USPTO and may pay the IB directly. Because IB requires Swiss francs, U.S. dollar payments collected by USPTO may convert to less than the prescribed Swiss amount; this can result in invitations from the IB to pay additional amounts. Any such additional payment must be made directly to the IB within the period set in the invitation to avoid abandonment under Article 8. To avoid invitations, applicants may authorize the IB to debit an IB account in the DM/1 fee payment section or use other IB authorization mechanisms (Administrative Instruction 801). Applicants may charge fees to a USPTO deposit account, but general authorization only applies to the transmittal fee, and international fees may not be paid through the USPTO after the date of payment of the transmittal fee. Renewal fees under Hague Rule 24 may not be paid through the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small and micro entity discounts and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmittal fee and certain parts of the individual designation fee (e.g., U.S. first part and second part) are discounted for small and micro entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment, by any party, of the exact small-entity transmittal fee will be treated as a written assertion of entitlement to small entity status (37 CFR 1.27). Micro entity certification may be signed by an authorized person and filed with the International Bureau; paying the small-entity first part of the U.S. individual designation fee to the IB is treated as a written assertion of small entity status. See 37 CFR 1.27(c)(3), 1.29(e), and MPEP §§ 509.* for establishment requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee Calculation Sheet and DM/1 form information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fee Calculation Sheet included with the DM/1 form specifies the amounts of the basic fees, publication fees, designation fees, and additional word fee (if description exceeds 100 words) and lists the level of the standard designation fee applicable to respective Contracting Parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DM/1 form includes items for fee payment and for specifying correspondence address for the IB and for the USPTO as office of indirect filing. Applicants should review the Fee Calculation Sheet and IB fee schedules/individual fee pages when determining payable amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation before the International Bureau and USPTO (Rule 3; 37 CFR 1.1041)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant or holder may have a representative before the International Bureau. Only one representative may be appointed in respect of a given international application or international registration; a partnership/firm indicated as representative is regarded as one representative. The appointment may be made in the international application or in a separate signed communication and must contain the representative's name and address (and email) as required by the Administrative Instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For representation before the USPTO as an office of indirect filing, the representative must be a practitioner registered (37 CFR 11.6) or granted limited recognition (37 CFR 11.9(a) or (b)). Such appointment must be in writing, signed by the applicant, give the practitioner power to act, and specify the name and registration or limited recognition number. An appointment in the international application pursuant to Rule 3(2) that complies with 37 CFR 1.1041(b) is effective as an appointment before the USPTO. IB provides forms DM/7 (appointment), DM/8 (recording change), and DM/9 (cancellation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence address for USPTO as office of indirect filing (37 CFR 1.1042)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant may specify a correspondence address for correspondence sent by the USPTO as an office of indirect filing. Where no such address is specified, the USPTO will use the address of the applicant’s appointed representative or, if none appointed, the address specified in Administrative Instruction 302.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DM/1 includes items for specifying addresses to be used by the IB. Where no correspondence information is included or it is irregular, the Office may use application data furnished through the USPTO electronic filing system (for example, the correspondence address associated with a customer number) until corrected by the applicant. If the appointment communication is irregular, the IB will notify the applicant and purported representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief from prescribed time limits for international design applications (37 CFR 1.1051; 35 U.S.C. 387)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's failure to act within prescribed time limits in connection with requirements pertaining to an international design application may be excused as to the United States upon a showing satisfactory to the Director of unintentional delay and under such conditions (including payment of fee) as the Director may prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.1051(a) must be accompanied by: (1) a copy of any IB invitation setting the prescribed time limit; (2) the required reply (unless previously filed); (3) the fee per § 1.17(m); (4) a certified copy of the originally filed international design application (or prior communication from IB) and translation if in another language; (5) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional (Director may require additional info); and (6) a terminal disclaimer (and fee per § 1.20(d)) dedicating to the public a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the delay period and applying to continuing patents claiming priority under 35 U.S.C. 120,121,365(c),386(c). If petition is refused, request for reconsideration/review must be filed within two months (may be extended under § 1.136). The required reply for a grantable petition may be: (1) filing of a continuing application (and, if not internationally registered, a grantable petition under § 1.1023(b) to accord a filing date) or (2) a grantable petition under § 1.1052 where application was filed with the Office as an office of indirect filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of an international design application to a U.S. design application (37 CFR 1.1052; 35 U.S.C. 384)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design application designating the United States that meets the requirements under § 1.53(b) for a filing date may, on petition, be converted to an application for a design patent under § 1.53(b) and accorded a filing date as provided therein. A petition must be accompanied by the fee set forth in § 1.17(t) and be filed prior to publication under Article 10(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion will not entitle applicant to a refund of the transmittal fee or any fee forwarded to the IB, or the application of any such fee toward U.S. filing fees. The converted application must include the basic filing, search, and examination fees, the inventor’s oath or declaration, and any required surcharge. A decision granting conversion is effective to convert the international design application to a U.S. design application for all purposes if granted prior to transmittal to the IB; if granted after transmittal, conversion is effective only for the U.S. designation. Conversion will not be granted in an abandoned international design application absent a grantable petition under § 1.1051. Converted applications are subject to regulations applicable to design applications filed under chapter 16.

rubrics_metrics.name: National processing, examination, and effects of international registration (35 U.S.C. 389; Hague Articles 10 & 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall cause an examination to be made pursuant to Title 35 of an international design application designating the United States. The international registration shall be published by the International Bureau and the IB shall send a copy of the publication to each designated Office. From the date of international registration, the international registration shall have at least the same effect in each designated Contracting Party as a regularly-filed application under the law of that Contracting Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All questions of substance and, unless treaty requires otherwise, procedures regarding an international design application designating the United States shall be determined as in the case of applications filed under chapter 16. Upon receipt of the IB publication under Article 10(3), the USPTO will establish an application file, send a filing receipt indicating U.S. application number and filing date, and make the U.S. application file publicly available via Patent Center after IB publication. The term "national" and "nonprovisional" application in USPTO rules includes an international design application for which the Office has received a copy of the international registration under Article 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal by designated Contracting Parties (Hague Article 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of any designated Contracting Party may refuse the effects, in part or in whole, of the international registration in its territory where the conditions for the grant of protection under the law of that Contracting Party are not met in respect of any or all of the industrial designs that are the subject of an international registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No Office may refuse the effects of an international registration on the ground that requirements relating to the form or contents of the international application that are provided for in the Hague Act or Regulations or are additional to, or different from, those requirements have not been satisfied under the law of the Contracting Party concerned. In practice, the USPTO will examine international design applications designating the United States pursuant to Title 35 and will not refuse based on treaty-form issues beyond national substantive law.
